title: Split EX into single-cycle integer ALU plus iterative DIV/REM unit
motivation:
All three baseline P&R seeds have the same critical path: ID/EX register ->
forward mux -> monolithic combinational ALU -> EX/MEM register (7.87 ns,
median 127.03 MHz). That ALU contains three soft 64-bit products plus fully
combinational signed/unsigned DIV and REM. The design uses 3704 Gowin ALU
carry cells and 9563 LUT4 for a 5-stage scalar core.

Measured evidence gathered for this hypothesis:
- Probe: identical bench RTL with only the DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU arms stubbed
  to 0, same synth.tcl + core_bench_si.sv + 3 nextpnr seeds. Fmax went
  148.32 / 150.58 / 139.10 MHz, median 148.3 vs 127.03 (+16.8%). LUT4 went
  9563 -> 4690 and ALU cells 3704 -> 308. The remaining critical path
  (6.74 ns) is ID/EX -> fwd mux -> ALU shift/logic mux -> final EX/MEM
  alu_result mux.
- A Verilator retirement trace of coremark.elf shows 2,922,016
  instructions between the start/stop markers, with ZERO
  DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU (93,960 MULs). Only 2 divides run in the whole program:
  1 before the bracket and 1 after it.
- Reference core v1 (read-only) made the same move from the same baseline
  ("Cold Multi-Cycle DIV/REM Unit"): Fmax 138 -> 160 MHz, LUT4
  10.2K -> 5.9K, fitness +16%, CoreMark cycles essentially unchanged.
  It was v1's largest single-step gain.

Why not other structural angles: a cycle-exact Python model of this
pipeline reproduced the measured stalled and unstalled cycle counts
exactly (3,483,582 / 4,302,170 / 3,675,518 / 4,491,485). With a decoupled
2-8 entry fetch queue plus empty-bypass, it only gets 4.49M -> 4.33M
cycles (-3.6%). Fetch bandwidth (0.78 words/cycle under the 22% imem
stall) is the ceiling. v1's elastic fetch skid buffer also regressed on
Fmax. Taking the divider off the universal EX path is the structural
change with by far the best measured payoff.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU out of the single-cycle ALU into a dedicated
multi-cycle divide unit that sits beside the ALU in EX, behind a
start/busy/done interlock. All RV32I ops, branches, loads/stores, jumps and
all four MUL variants stay single-cycle and bit-identical. Do NOT reshape
or re-time the multiplier: two v1 attempts dropped Fmax to 95-100 MHz.

1. div_unit (new): radix-2 restoring divider with one 33-bit
   subtract/compare plus shift per cycle. It takes absolute-value operands
   for signed ops and applies sign fixup at the end. Divide-by-zero and
   INT_MIN/-1 are resolved at start with no iteration, returning
   0xFFFFFFFF/dividend or INT_MIN/0 exactly as today. Result and done are
   registered outputs.
   Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, keep the same start/busy/done handshake but
   use a fixed short latency (1-2 busy cycles) returning the existing ALTOPS
   formulas (moved here from alu.sv). This keeps insn/liveness within the
   depth-20 formal budget while still proving the stall/ordering logic.
2. EX (ex_stage) behavior while a divide is in EX:
   - On its first EX cycle, latch the post-forward rs1/rs2 values and start
     the unit. These latched values also feed RVFI rs1_rdata/rs2_rdata,
     because forwarding sources drain while the divide waits.
   - While busy, on every non-dmem-stall cycle, EX/MEM captures a bubble
     (valid=0, reg_write=0, no mem op). This makes older instructions
     retire exactly once.
   - On done, which stays sticky until EX/MEM can accept (!dmem_stall),
     EX/MEM captures the divide's full metadata and result.
   - Result injection must not add a LUT level to the critical
     ALU -> EX/MEM path. Merge it with the existing JAL/JALR link-value
     mux: alu_result_q <= use_alt ? alt_val : alu_result, where
     use_alt = is_jump | div_done and alt_val = div_done ? div_q : pc+4.
     Both selects and alt_val come only from registers, so the final mux
     stays 2:1 as today.
3. hazard_unit: new ex_div_busy input. While it is high, hold the PC and
   ID/EX (stall, not flush). Keep dmem_stall priority unchanged. A divide
   never redirects and is never a load, so load-use and redirect logic are
   untouched.
4. decoder/core_pkg: add a ctrl bit is_div. Set it only inside the
   already-validated funct7=0000001 arm when funct3[2]=1, so EX tests one
   registered bit instead of decoding alu_op. is_illegal defaults remain
   untouched.

Expected result: CoreMark bracketed cycles stay about 4.49M. Any change
should only be LFSR stall-phase noise from the one pre-bracket DIV now
taking ~34 cycles. A larger change means an interlock bug. Median Fmax
should rise to about 142-148 MHz, a bit under the 148.3 probe because of
the small divider and control added back. That gives fitness of roughly
282.82 -> ~320-330 iter/s.

title: Fetch-stage predecode + 64-entry bimodal BHT (zero-bubble correctly-predicted branches/JAL)
motivation:
The core has no branch prediction: next_pc is always pc+4, and every taken
BRANCH/JAL/JALR redirects from EX. IF and ID share one cycle (imem is read
combinationally from the PC register and there is no IF/ID flop), so each taken
control transfer costs exactly 1 bubble.

I measured this on the real fitness workload. The existing cosim_sim
(--istall --dstall, default seed) reproduces the logged 4,491,485 cycles. I
counted the RVFI stream between the 0x10000100 and 0x10000104 markers:
  - 2,922,015 instructions retired; CPI 1.537.
  - Branches are 18.1% of instructions. 294,425 of them are taken (10.1%).
    Backward branches are taken 82% of the time.
  - JAL: 49,367 (1.7%). JALR: 13,735 (0.47%), all of them returns.
  - Taken control transfers total 357,527, i.e. 357k bubble cycles, about 8.0%
    of all cycles. This is the second-largest overhead after bus stalls.
    Load-use accounts for 204k.
I replayed that trace through several predictors (cost = number of mispredicted
control transfers, 1 cycle each):
  - No prediction (today): 357.5k.
  - Static backward-taken/forward-not-taken: 125k.
  - Bimodal 2-bit, 32 entries: 69k. 64 entries: 65k. 256 entries: 58k.
    JAL is always predicted taken in all of these; JALR is not predicted.
  - Adding a 4-entry return stack saves only about 14k more (0.3%). Not worth
    a 32-bit compare on the forwarded JALR path.
  - gshare only beats bimodal at 1024 entries or more (38k). Too big for a
    design sitting at 9563 LUT4 against a 10k target.
So a small bimodal table plus fetch-time target computation captures about 82%
of the available control-flow gain. It needs no target storage and no tags.
Each correctly predicted taken branch saves exactly 1 cycle, even with random
imem stalls. The target fetch simply moves one cycle earlier, and the stall
probability on that fetch is unchanged.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Predict at fetch using the instruction that the fetch cycle already has
combinationally (imem_data). Verify in EX. Keep the 1-cycle mispredict penalty.

1. IF-stage predecode (if_stage.sv)
   - From the raw imem_data, detect BRANCH (opcode 1100011) and JAL
     (opcode 1101111).
   - Select the B-immediate or the J-immediate.
   - Compute pred_target = pc + imm. A 30-bit add on [31:2] is enough because
     pc[1:0] = 0 and imm[0] = 0.
   - Never predict when imm[1] = 1, i.e. instr[8] for B-type or instr[21] for
     J-type. That target would be misaligned, and EX's existing misalign trap
     must see a non-taken prediction.
   - Never predict JALR.
2. BHT (inside if_stage.sv)
   - 64 x 2-bit saturating counters. Use a flop array with synchronous reset
     to 2'b01. That keeps it deterministic for formal and cosim and avoids
     depending on SSRAM/LUT-RAM support in nextpnr-himbaechel.
   - Index with pc[7:2]. Read combinationally at fetch.
   - pred_taken_raw = is_jal_pd | (is_br_pd & bht[pc[7:2]][1]), and suppressed
     when imm[1] = 1.
   - One write port driven from EX.
3. next_pc
   - PC priority stays: redirect > stall > advance.
   - Advance = pred_taken_raw ? pred_target : pc+4. Keep the mux ordering as
     redirect ? redirect_target : (pred ? pred_target : pc+4), so the late
     EX-redirect signal still drives only the outermost mux level.
   - The prediction is naturally ignored whenever stall_if holds the PC
     (load-use, imem stall, dmem stall). The same PC is re-predicted from the
     refetched word next cycle. This matters for formal, where imem_data is a
     free value every cycle.
4. New pipeline fields (IF/ID bundle -> ID/EX register)
   - pred_taken: MUST be gated with the bundle's valid, i.e.
     pred_taken_raw & !(flush || redirect). A bubble captured during an imem
     stall or a flush must carry pred_taken = 0; otherwise EX would fire a
     spurious redirect.
   - bht_ctr[1:0]: the counter value read at fetch, used for the update.
   - alt_target = pred_taken ? pc+4 : pc+imm. This is the "other" path EX
     redirects to if it disagrees.
   - The ID/EX flush/reset path already zeroes the whole struct. That is
     required for all three fields.
5. EX (ex_stage.sv)
   - actual = (branch_taken | is_jump) & !misalign_fault. This is exactly
     today's redirect expression.
   - redirect = actual ^ in.pred_taken. This is now a mispredict signal. The
     hazard unit and if_stage keep consuming `redirect` unchanged, so
     flush_if/flush_id behave exactly as today: only on a mispredict.
   - redirect_target = in.ctrl.is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],1'b0} : in.alt_target.
     JALR is never predicted. A predicted-taken instruction that disagrees
     always goes to pc+4, and a non-predicted branch/JAL goes to pc+imm, both
     taken from alt_target. This takes the EX pc+imm adder off the
     redirect->PC path, which offsets the extra XOR level.
   - pc_next / RVFI pc_wdata logic is unchanged.
   - BHT update: when in.valid & in.ctrl.is_branch, write
     bht[in.pc[7:2]] <= branch_cond ? sat_inc(in.bht_ctr) : sat_dec(in.bht_ctr).
     Repeated writes while EX is held by a dmem stall are idempotent.
6. core.sv: wire the BHT write port (we, index, data) from ex_stage to
   if_stage.

Correctness argument
- pred_target is derived from the same instruction bits that are captured into
  ID/EX in that cycle. So a predicted-taken BRANCH/JAL always has the correct
  target; the only possible wrong outcome is direction. Counters may hold any
  value without affecting architectural state.
- Exactly one wrong-path instruction can exist (the one in fetch), and the
  existing flush_if/flush_id machinery kills it, as it does today.
- rvfi_order, pc_fwd/pc_bwd, unique, liveness and ill are unaffected. Trap
  discipline is unchanged: a misaligned target is never predicted, and a
  predicted instruction that faults redirects to pc+4.

Expected effect
- Cycles: about 4.49M -> 4.20M (-6.5%), i.e. +7.0% iterations/cycle.
- Fmax: the added fetch path is imem_data (an LFSR flop in the FPGA bench) ->
  1-level predecode/imm mux -> 30-bit carry chain -> 2-level PC mux, plus a
  parallel pc -> 64:1 counter mux. Both should sit well under the current
  7.87 ns ALU-limited critical path. The EX redirect path gains an XOR but
  loses the pc+imm adder on redirect_target.
- Area: about +150-200 LUT4 and about +165 FF (128 BHT flops + 33 new ID/EX
  bits). That stays under the 10k LUT target.

title: Pre-decoded one-hot ALU controls registered in ID/EX (no opcode decode in EX)
motivation:
After the DIV/REM split the core runs at 161.26 MHz median and 4,491,817
bracketed CoreMark cycles. I re-ran synth + nextpnr on the current

  variants beat 161.26. The mean across them is ~177 MHz (+10%).

  the limiters become routing-dominated ~5.0-6.0 ns paths elsewhere

  gives the identical 4,491,817 bracketed cycles, all five CRCs match

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Remove all ALU opcode decoding from the EX stage by pre-decoding alu_op in
ID into a registered one-hot control bundle. Pipeline timing, forwarding,
hazards, the div_unit protocol, RVFI, and the CoreMark cycle count
(4,491,817) stay exactly as they are. Implement it as the measured e1
prototype, without extra tweaks. Measurements show that unrelated edits
re-roll the ABC/P&R result.

1. core_pkg.sv. Add a packed struct before id_ex_t:
     typedef struct packed {
       logic sub;        // SUB, SLT, SLTU: b inverted + carry-in
       logic sra;        // right-shift fill = a[31]
       logic mul_a_sgn;  // MULH, MULHSU
       logic mul_b_sgn;  // MULH
       logic sel_sum;    // ADD, SUB
       logic sel_and; logic sel_or; logic sel_xor;
       logic sel_slt; logic sel_sltu;
       logic sel_sll; logic sel_sr;   // SRL, SRA
       logic sel_b;      // LUI
       logic sel_mul_lo; // MUL
       logic sel_mul_hi; // MULH, MULHU, MULHSU
     } alu_ctl_t;
   Add `alu_ctl_t alu_ctl;` to id_ex_t, right after ctrl. Keep the ALU_*
   constants and ctrl_t.alu_op unchanged. The decoder is untouched.
2. alu.sv. Three modules in the one file:
   - alu_predecode(op -> ctl): ctl = '0, then a case on the ALU_*
     constants sets the bits above. DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU/default leave all
     zeros.
   - alu_core(ctl, a, b -> out):
       sum  = {1'b0,a} + {1'b0, b ^ {32{sub}}} + sub      (33-bit)
       lt_s = (a[31]^b[31]) ? a[31] : sum[31];  lt_u = !sum[32]
       sll  = a << b[4:0]
       sr   = low 32 bits of $signed({sra & a[31], a}) >>> b[4:0]
       prod = $signed({mul_a_sgn&a[31], a}) * $signed({mul_b_sgn&b[31], b})
              (66-bit signed; mul_lo = prod[31:0], mul_hi = prod[63:32])
       out  = OR of ({32{sel_x}} & term_x) over sum/and/or/xor/sll/sr/b/
              mul_lo/mul_hi, | {31'b0, sel_slt&lt_s | sel_sltu&lt_u}
     Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS keep today's formulas bit-for-bit:
       mul_lo = (a+b)^32'h5876063e
       mul_hi = mul_b_sgn ? (a+b)^32'hf6583fb7
              : mul_a_sgn ? (a-b)^32'hecfbe137
              :             (a+b)^32'h949ce5e8
   - alu(op, a, b -> out): the existing port list, chaining alu_predecode
     into alu_core. test/test_alu.py's toplevel and all vectors keep
     working unchanged.
3. id_stage.sv. `alu_predecode u_alu_pd(.op(dec_alu_op), .ctl(...))` and
   `reg_q.alu_ctl <= alu_ctl_decoded;` inside the existing ID/EX
   capture. The existing reset/flush-to-'0 zeroes it on bubbles (all
   selects 0 -> ALU out 0).
4. ex_stage.sv. Replace `alu u_alu(.op(in.ctrl.alu_op), ...)` with
   `alu_core u_alu(.ctl(in.alu_ctl), ...)`. Keep the rest unchanged:

   alt_val 2:1 merge (JAL/JALR link, div_done result), branch compare,

implementation_notes:
# Implementation notes — Pre-decoded one-hot ALU controls in ID/EX

## What changed (matches the hypothesis plan)

- `rtl/core_pkg.sv`: new packed `alu_ctl_t` (sub, sra, mul_a_sgn, mul_b_sgn,
  sel_sum, sel_and, sel_or, sel_xor, sel_slt, sel_sltu, sel_sll, sel_sr,
  sel_b, sel_mul_lo, sel_mul_hi) declared before `id_ex_t`. `id_ex_t` gets
  `alu_ctl_t alu_ctl` right after `ctrl`. ALU_* constants, `ctrl_t.alu_op`
  and the decoder are unchanged.
- `rtl/alu.sv`: three modules.
  - `alu_predecode(op -> ctl)`: `ctl = '0`, then a case on ALU_*.
    DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU/default leave all zeros.
  - `alu_core(ctl, a, b -> out)`: one 33-bit add/sub
    (`{0,a} + {0, b^{32{sub}}} + sub`), `lt_s = (a[31]^b[31]) ? a[31] : sum[31]`,
    `lt_u = !sum[32]`, `a << b[4:0]`, 33-bit `>>>` with fill `sra & a[31]`,
    one signed product of the 33-bit sign/zero-extended operands, and an
    AND-OR result merge. Under `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` the MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU
    formulas are the same as before bit for bit, with MULH/MULHSU/MULHU picked by
    mul_b_sgn / mul_a_sgn.
  - `alu(op, a, b -> out)`: same ports as before, chaining predecode into core
    (used by `test_alu.py` only; the core no longer instantiates it).
- `rtl/id_stage.sv`: `alu_predecode u_alu_pd(.op(dec_alu_op), ...)` and
  `reg_q.alu_ctl <= alu_ctl_decoded;` inside the existing ID/EX capture.
  Reset, flush and stall behave the same as for the other fields; a bubble has
  all selects 0, so the ALU output is 0.
- `rtl/ex_stage.sv`: `alu u_alu(.op(in.ctrl.alu_op))` is now
  `alu_core u_alu(.ctl(in.alu_ctl))`. Nothing else in EX changed.
- `test/test_alu.py`: new corner tests `slt_sltu_corners` (0x80000000 vs
  0x7fffffff both ways, equal operands, 0xffffffff vs 0, ...),
  `add_sub_corners` (SUB/ADD wraparound), `mul_high_corners` (MUL/MULH/MULHU/
  MULHSU on INT_MIN*INT_MIN, 0xffffffff^2, INT_MIN*0xffffffff both ways,
  0x7fffffff*0x80000000 both ways, ...), `rv32i_vectors` (every RV32I op against
  a Python reference on corner and random pairs, which guards the one-hot merge),
  and `div_ops_output_zero`.

## Deviations

- The product operands are written as explicit 66-bit sign extensions
  (`{{34{mul_a_sgn & a[31]}}, a}`) rather than 33-bit `$signed(...)` operands
  in a 66-bit context. The two are the same in Verilog. The explicit form keeps
  `verilator -Wall` free of WIDTH warnings, and Yosys `wreduce` trims the
  redundant sign bits, so it still maps to one MULT36X36.
- `/* verilator lint_off DECLFILENAME */` wraps `alu_predecode` / `alu_core`
  because `alu.sv` now holds more than one module.

## Concerns

- The literal lint command `verilator ... cores/bench/rtl/*.sv` (plain shell
  glob) now fails with "Reference to 'alu_ctl_t' before declaration", because
  the glob sorts `alu.sv` before `core_pkg.sv` and the new typedef is used in a
  port. Every real tool path forces `core_pkg.sv` first: orchestrator lint,
  `implement.py`, `make lint`, `test/cosim/build.sh`, `synth.tcl` and
  `formal/run_all.sh`. With that order, lint is clean with and without
  `-DRISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` (0 warnings). The file was not renamed, because that
  would change the synth read order and the test source lists.
- The Fmax gain is P&R/ABC-noise-sensitive, as the hypothesis itself says. I did
  not run nextpnr locally.

## Local verification

- Lint (core_pkg.sv first, `-Wall -Wno-MULTITOP`): clean, with and without
  ALTOPS.
- cocotb: test_alu (19 alu tests + 15 div_unit tests), test_decoder (31) and
  test_pipeline (17) all pass.
- **Formal (`formal/run_all.sh`, nret=1 / checks_si.cfg): 53 passed, 0 failed**
  on the first attempt.
- Verilator CoreMark (`--bench --istall --dstall`, 2K, -O3, ITERATIONS=10):
  bracketed cycles **4,491,817** (identical to before). seedcrc 0xe9f5,
  crclist 0xe714, crcmatrix 0x1fd7, crcstate 0x8e3a, crcfinal 0xfcaf,
  "Correct operation validated.", oob=false.
- RVFI cosim vs Python ISS: selftest passed (115 retired); CoreMark passed
  (2,937,037 retired).
- Yosys `synth_gowin` (same synth.tcl, core_bench_si.sv), HEAD -> this change:
  LUT4 2304 -> 2340, MUX2_LUT5 467 -> 358, ALU (carry) 386 -> 355,
  MULT36X36 1 -> 1. This local Yosys counts cells differently from the 5116
  figure in the hypothesis, but the direction matches: fewer mux levels and
  carry cells in total.
lesson: - 2026-09-26 hyp-20260926-001-r3s0 (regression, +4.77%): Pre-decoding alu_op in ID into a registered one-hot alu_ctl_t (AND-OR result merge, one shared add/sub, one 33x33 product) is cycle-neutral (4,491,817) and passed formal/cosim first try, but it landed at only ~169 MHz, not the prototype's 199 MHz, because once the EX opcode decode is gone the limiter moves to routing-dominated ~5-6 ns paths (regfile bypass->ID/EX, hazard enable fan-out, div_unit) that re-roll with every netlist; it was a "regression" only because it lost to the same-round I-fetch replay store (+22.1%), so stack it on that base as a small, safe gain, and budget from the low end of a multi-variant P&R spread, not the best single prototype.

title: Stall-only I-fetch replay store with registered next-PC lookahead
motivation:
After the DIV/REM split, the largest remaining cycle loss is the instruction
bus, not the datapath. Today `io_imemReady=0` is a global frontend stall:
hazard_unit sets imem_stall = !imem_ready, the PC holds, and IF pushes a NOP
bubble into ID/EX. The fitness cosim drives about 22% random accept-fail on
imem every cycle. This loses fetch cycles even in CoreMark's hot loops,
where the same few hundred instruction words are fetched millions of times.

Measured on the current core (this tree's RTL rebuilt with
test/cosim/build.sh, NRET=1, coremark.elf, --bench, default LFSR seed;
bracketed cycles between the 0x10000100 and 0x10000104 markers):
  - --istall --dstall: 4,491,817 cycles. This matches the logged current
    best exactly.
  - --dstall only:     3,675,475
  - --istall only:     4,302,144
  - no stalls:         3,483,582
Random imem stalls therefore cost about 816k cycles, 18% of the fitness
run. That is the largest single overhead: taken-branch bubbles are about
357k and load-use is about 204k.

The timed region is 2,922,015 retirements over only 1,669 unique PCs, in
0x150..0x3988. Direct-mapped hit rates on the retired-PC stream with full
tags:

  entries   hit rate
       64      71.5%
      128      83.3%
      256      93.8%
      512      97.0%
     1024      98.9%

Reference core v1 (read-only) validated this mechanism. Its stall-only
replay table cut cycles 4.23M -> 3.46M. It lost Fmax only while the table
read and tag compare sat combinationally on the same-cycle fetch-ready
path. The registered-lookahead form below fixed that and was v1's largest
post-DIV gain. Things v1 showed not to do: fetch skid queues or decoupled
fetch buffers (permanent muxes on the zero-wait path) and small
combinational tables (64 entries: 97 MHz).

PROTOTYPE, MEASURED END-TO-END with the real flow. Scratch copy of
cores/bench/rtl with exactly the if_stage/core changes below; nothing in
the repo was modified.

CoreMark cycles (--istall --dstall, CRCs valid, "Correct operation
validated"):

  variant                        cycles      vs 4,491,817
  128 entries                    3,808,685   -15.2%
  256 entries                    3,724,565   -17.1%
  512 entries                    3,699,911   -17.6%
  1024 entries                   3,683,593   -18.0%
  floor (dstall-only reference)  3,675,475   -18.2%

- LFSR seeds 12345 and 987654321: the reference measures 4.494M / 4.493M,
  and the 512-entry replay 3.6995M / 3.6993M. The gain is seed-robust.
- No-stall run: 3,483,582, identical to the reference, so the zero-wait
  behaviour is unchanged.
- Correctness: the RVFI stream was diffed field-by-field against
  test/cosim/reference.py (run_cosim.compare) with the sim running
  --istall --dstall. It passes on selftest.elf (3 stall configs) and on
  all 2,937,037 CoreMark retirements.
- FPGA flow (fpga/scripts/synth.tcl with core_bench_si.sv, then
  nextpnr_run.sh seeds 1/2/3):
    reference core:  176.12 / 161.26 / 161.16 MHz, median 161.26
                     (reproduces the log exactly), LUT4 5116
    512-entry replay: 170.44 / 150.76 / 159.85 MHz, median 159.85,
                     LUT4 5160
- Fitness: 10 / 3,699,911 x 159.85e6 = 432.0, versus 359.01 (+20.3%).

Why Fmax is unchanged: fpga/core_bench_si.sv ties io_imemReady=1. The
replay storage, candidate registers and lookahead are consumed only on
!imem_ready cycles, so they constant-fold away. The synthesized netlist
keeps no rp_*/cand_* nets, and the DFF count differs by 1. The small
LUT/MUX2_LUT5 delta is ABC re-mapping of u_id logic that is functionally
identical. The design is still kept timing-clean for a real stalling bus:
  - The table is read synchronously, addressed by the next PC (the shape
    of one 512x36 BSRAM).
  - The only same-cycle addition to the fetch-ready path is one OR with a
    flop.

Add a small L0 "replay store" inside IF. It serves an instruction only on
cycles where the external imem does not accept the fetch, and only for a PC
it has seen before. Instruction memory is read-only in this contract: cosim
keeps separate imem/dmem arrays, stores never reach imem, and FENCE.I is a
NOP. A cached word therefore can never be stale, and no invalidation beyond
reset is needed. When io_imemReady=1, IF uses io_imemData exactly as today.

1. Replay array (inside if_stage.sv; no new file)
   - 512 entries, index pc[10:2].
   - Per entry: valid bit, tag pc[31:11], 32-bit word.
   - valid[] is a flop vector cleared on reset. The tag and data arrays are
     resetless and never consumed without valid.
   - Fill on every imem_ready cycle at pc[10:2].
2. Registered next-PC lookahead
   - pc_d = redirect ? redirect_target : (!stall ? pc+4 : pc). This is the
     same priority as the PC flop.
   - At each edge, register cand_pc_q <= pc_d, plus cand_hit_q and
     cand_instr_q from the table entry at pc_d.
   - Fill bypass: when imem_ready && pc_d == pc (PC held while the live
     word arrived), the candidate is imem_data and hit=1.
   - A same-cycle fill to the lookahead index for a different PC is benign
     under the tag check, because the words are immutable.
3. Fetch select (the only same-cycle change)
   - fetch_ready = imem_ready || (cand_hit_q && cand_pc_q == pc)
   - instr_word  = imem_ready ? imem_data : cand_instr_q
   - out.instr / out.valid use instr_word. flush/redirect still force the
     NOP exactly as today.
4. Hazard unit: imem_stall = !fetch_ready instead of !io_imemReady.
   - stall_if, flush_if, load-use detection (which now sees the replayed
     word's rs1/rs2) and PC advance behave exactly as on a live fetch.
   - Redirect, dmem-stall, load-use and div-busy priorities are unchanged.
   - io_imemAddr may advance on a cycle the bus did not accept. This
     matches the per-cycle accept model in cosim.

Prototype RTL that produced the numbers above (IDX=9). Port list
additions: input imem_ready, output fetch_ready. The PC flop and next_pc
logic are unchanged.

  pc_d = redirect ? redirect_target : (!stall ? pc + 32'd4 : pc);
  logic [511:0] rp_valid;  logic [20:0] rp_tag [0:511];
  logic [31:0]  rp_data [0:511];
  fidx = pc[10:2];  lidx = pc_d[10:2];
  always_ff @(posedge clock) begin            // resetless payload
    if (imem_ready) begin rp_tag[fidx] <= pc[31:11];
                          rp_data[fidx] <= imem_data; end
    cand_instr_q <= (imem_ready && pc_d == pc) ? imem_data : rp_data[lidx];
  end
  always_ff @(posedge clock) begin
    if (reset) begin rp_valid <= '0; cand_hit_q <= 0; cand_pc_q <= 0; end
    else begin
      if (imem_ready) rp_valid[fidx] <= 1'b1;
      cand_pc_q  <= pc_d;
      cand_hit_q <= (imem_ready && pc_d == pc)
                 || (rp_valid[lidx] && rp_tag[lidx] == pc_d[31:11]);
    end
  end
  fetch_ready = imem_ready || (cand_hit_q && cand_pc_q == pc);
  instr_word  = imem_ready ? imem_data : cand_instr_q;
  out.instr   = (flush || redirect) ? 32'h0000_0013 : instr_word;

  - Connect u_if.imem_ready to io_imemReady.

title: Fetch predecode + 64-entry bimodal BHT on the post-DIV-split core
motivation:
The core has no branch prediction. next_pc is always pc+4, and every taken
BRANCH/JAL/JALR redirects from EX with a 1-cycle bubble (IF and ID share a
cycle because imem_data is decoded combinationally). On the fitness trace
(2.92M retired between the markers, 4,491,485 bracketed cycles), 357.5k
taken control transfers cost about 8% of all cycles.

hyp-20260926-003-r1s2 measured this predictor on the pre-split baseline:
4.49M -> 4.20M cycles, with no Fmax loss there. It scored "regression" only
because the DIV/REM split (359.01) won the same round. LESSONS.md says to
re-apply it on the post-split core. I prototyped it on the current bench
RTL (scratch copy, not committed) and measured it with the real eval flow:
  - cosim (--bench --istall --dstall): 4,491,485 -> 4,201,740 bracketed
    cycles (-6.45%). All CoreMark CRCs match, "Correct operation
    validated". A BHT-size sweep gave 32: 4,203,446; 64: 4,201,740;
    128: 4,202,272; 256: 4,193,175. 64 entries is the knee.
  - Yosys: LUT1-4 5116 -> ~5160. It is tiny now that the divider is gone.
  - nextpnr, same synth.tcl/core_bench_si.sv. Current core, seeds 1-7:
    176.1 161.3 161.2 142.9 163.2 162.5 170.4 (median 162.5). Prototype,
    seeds 1-6: 147.2 153.9 159.8 152.3 150.5 158.3 (median ~153). On every
    seed, the critical path is the same pre-existing EX path: ID/EX alu_op
    -> ALU result-select mux tree -> EX/MEM. The predictor logic is never
    on it; the ~5% loss is placement perturbation of that path.
  - Net at median-of-3 seeds 1-3 (153.94 MHz): 10/4,201,740 x 153.94e6 =
    366.4 vs 359.01, i.e. +2%. If P&R lands the ALU path as it does today
    (~161 MHz), the result is +7%.
In a controlled comparison, removing `redirect` from the IF NOP/valid mux
(keeping only imem_stall there) was functionally identical but WORSE
(median 140 MHz). The imem_data -> load-use -> ID/EX clock-enable path then
became critical. Keep the existing kill = flush || redirect structure.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Predict BRANCH/JAL at fetch from the raw imem_data word, verify in EX, and
keep today's 1-cycle penalty for mispredicts. JALR stays unpredicted.

IF (if_stage.sv):
  - Predecode from imem_data:
      is_br  = opcode==1100011 && funct3[2:1] != 2'b01
               (only the valid branch funct3 values)
      is_jal = opcode==1101111
    pimm = instr[2] ? J-imm : B-imm; pred_target = pc + pimm.
  - BHT: 64 x 2-bit saturating counters. Use a flop array with synchronous
    reset to 2'b01 (deterministic for formal/cosim, no LUT-RAM
    inference). Index with pc[7:2] and read combinationally, i.e. FF -> mux,
    in parallel with predecode.
  - pred_raw = (is_jal | (is_br & ctr[1])) & !pimm[1]. Never predict an
    imm[1]=1 target, so EX's misalign trap only ever sees unpredicted
    instructions.
  - The PC always_ff keeps its priority: reset > redirect > !stall.
    Advance with pc <= pred_raw ? pred_target : pc+4. Redirect stays the
    outermost select. On a stall the prediction is dropped and the same PC
    is re-predicted from the re-fetched word.
  - Bundle: pred_taken = pred_raw & !(flush||redirect). This MUST be gated:
    bubbles carry pred_taken=0, or EX would fire a false redirect. Also
    bht_ctr = ctr, and alt_target = pred_raw ? pc+4 : pred_target.
ID (id_stage.sv): capture pred_taken / bht_ctr / alt_target in ID/EX. The
existing reset/flush-to-'0 zeroes them on bubbles.
EX (ex_stage.sv):
  - actual   = (branch_taken | is_jump) & !misalign_fault
    (today's redirect expression).
  - redirect = actual ^ in.pred_taken. This now means "mispredict". The
    hazard unit, if_stage and the dmem-stall/div-busy interlocks consume
    it unchanged.
  - redirect_target = is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],1'b0} : in.alt_target.
  - pc_next, RVFI and the misalign trap logic are unchanged.
  - BHT update, REGISTERED one cycle after EX. This keeps the slow
    forwarded-compare branch_cond off the 128-flop BHT write fan-in:
      we_q    <= in.valid & in.ctrl.is_branch
      idx_q   <= in.pc[7:2]
      wdata_q <= branch_cond ? sat_inc(in.bht_ctr) : sat_dec(in.bht_ctr)
    Repeated writes while EX is held (dmem stall) are idempotent.
core.sv: wire bht_we/bht_widx/bht_wdata from u_ex to u_if.
hazard_unit.sv: no change.

Interaction with the div_unit interlock: a divide is never predicted
(pred_taken=0), so redirect is 0 while ex_div_busy holds PC and ID/EX. The
held ID/EX keeps its prediction fields.

Correctness: pred_target comes from the same instruction bits that are
captured into ID/EX that cycle, so the only possible error is direction.
At most one wrong-path instruction exists, and today's flush_if/flush_id
kills it. rvfi_order, pc_fwd/pc_bwd, unique, liveness and ill are unaffected.

Expected: cycles -6.45% (measured), Fmax neutral to -5% (P&R perturbation
of the pre-existing ALU critical path). Net about +2..+7%.

title: D-side stall-only load replay cache (256-entry, registered lookahead) + 1-entry posted store buffer
motivation:
The I-fetch replay store (r3s1, +22.1%) removed nearly all imem-stall
cycles. The largest bus overhead left is now the DATA bus. Today any
io_dmemReady=0 cycle with a LOAD/STORE in EX/MEM freezes the whole
pipeline. The fitness cosim drives ~22% random dmem refusals, and the FPGA
bench and formal wrapper both tie io_dmemReady to 1.

I measured this on the current cores/bench RTL (test/cosim/build.sh, NRET=1,
coremark.elf --bench; bracketed cycles):
  --istall --dstall : 3,699,911   (= logged current best)
  --istall only     : 3,508,312
  --dstall only     : 3,675,475
  no stalls         : 3,483,582
So dstall costs 191.6k cycles, 5.2% of the fitness run. It is now the
largest overhead not already targeted by another slot: taken-branch
bubbles (~357k) are the predictor slot's job, and load-use (~204k) cannot
be removed without putting dmem on the EX critical path.

RVFI trace of the timed region: 2,922,015 insns, 544,852 loads, 139,630
stores, only 611 unique data words. Loads are 80% of dmem accesses.
Direct-mapped word-cache load hit rate (full tag, stores merge/allocate):
64: 72.6%, 128: 94.4%, 256: 97.2%, 512: 98.0%, 1024: 99.5%.

Data memory has exactly one master (this core) and the harness keeps imem
and dmem separate. A cache updated by every store is therefore coherent by
construction. It is a real (stall-only) D-cache, the data-side twin of the
accepted I-side replay store. It is not a harness exploit: the core never
reads io_dmemRData on a cycle where io_dmemReady=0.

with exactly the changes below; nothing in the repo was modified.
  CoreMark cycles (--istall --dstall), all 5 CRCs match, "Correct
  operation validated.", oob=false:
    current                                 3,699,911
    64-entry cache + store buffer           3,552,001
    128-entry                               3,519,130
    256-entry  (PROPOSED)                   3,514,311   (-5.02%)
    512-entry                               3,513,172
    256-entry, NO store buffer              3,551,121   (buffer is worth 36.8k)
    floor (istall-only reference)           3,508,312
  - Seed-robust. LFSR seeds 12345 / 987654321 / 42 give base 3,699,522 /
    3,699,331 / 3,699,622 and prototype 3,514,379 / 3,514,233 / 3,514,316.
  - Zero-wait run is unchanged (3,483,582). --istall-only is unchanged
    (3,508,312). --dstall-only drops 3,675,475 -> 3,489,791.
  - Full RVFI diff vs test/cosim/reference.py, streamed per retirement
    with run_cosim.compare(). PASS on all 2,937,037 CoreMark retirements
    with --istall --dstall and with --dstall --seed 777. PASS on
    selftest.elf with none / --istall / --dstall / both, and with 4
    extra seeds.
  - cocotb. The existing test_pipeline suite passes 20/20 once
    div_done_held_by_dmem_stall uses a cold LW instead of a SW as its
    stalling op (see changes); the SW is now posted, which is intended.
    A scratch random-program stress test also passes. It runs 40 random
    LW/LH/LHU/LB/LBU/SW/SH/SB/ADD mixes over three index-aliasing base
    addresses x 4 stall profiles up to 70% dstall, drives POISON on

    all-ready run. It catches injected bugs: no cache update on store,
    no same-word lookahead bypass, no drain priority.
  - FPGA (fpga/scripts/synth.tcl with core_bench_si.sv, then

    sb_valid_q aliases to GND and no dc_*/cand_*/sb_* cells survive.

      base : 162.23 / 172.03 / 160.80 MHz (median 162.23 = logged)

io_dmemReady=0 cycle with a LOAD/STORE in EX/MEM freezes the whole
pipeline. The fitness cosim drives ~22% random dmem refusals, and the FPGA
bench and formal wrapper both tie io_dmemReady to 1.

I measured this on the current cores/bench RTL (test/cosim/build.sh, NRET=1,
coremark.elf --bench; bracketed cycles):
  --istall --dstall : 3,699,911   (= logged current best)
  --istall only     : 3,508,312
  --dstall only     : 3,675,475
  no stalls         : 3,483,582
So dstall costs 191.6k cycles, 5.2% of the fitness run. It is now the
largest overhead not already targeted by another slot: taken-branch
bubbles (~357k) are the predictor slot's job, and load-use (~204k) cannot
be removed without putting dmem on the EX critical path.

RVFI trace of the timed region: 2,922,015 insns, 544,852 loads, 139,630
stores, only 611 unique data words. Loads are 80% of dmem accesses.
Direct-mapped word-cache load hit rate (full tag, stores merge/allocate):
64: 72.6%, 128: 94.4%, 256: 97.2%, 512: 98.0%, 1024: 99.5%.

Data memory has exactly one master (this core) and the harness keeps imem
and dmem separate. A cache updated by every store is therefore coherent by
construction. It is a real (stall-only) D-cache, the data-side twin of the
accepted I-side replay store. It is not a harness exploit: the core never
reads io_dmemRData on a cycle where io_dmemReady=0.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add two stall-only structures to MEM, both consumed ONLY on cycles where
the external bus cannot serve the MEM-stage access. With io_dmemReady tied
to 1 (FPGA bench, formal wrapper) every new state bit either has a constant
D input or feeds only dead logic, so the netlist folds back to today's.

Definitions (mem_stage, combinational):
  ld       = ctrl.mem_read  && !mem_misalign      (= today's dmem_ren)
  st       = ctrl.mem_write && !mem_misalign
  bus_free = dmem_ready && !sb_valid_q    (bus serves the MEM op this cycle)
  st_done  = st && !sb_valid_q    (store written directly, or posted)
  ld_fill  = ld && bus_free
  ld_word  = bus_free ? dmem_rdata : cand_data_q
  mem_ready = bus_free || (ld && cand_hit_q) || st_done
hazard_unit's dmem_stall becomes !mem_ready && ex_mem_mem_op (replacing
!dmem_ready). All other stall/flush/hold equations and priorities stay.

1. Posted store buffer (1 entry): sb_valid_q, sb_addr_q, sb_wdata_q
   (replicated lanes), sb_wmask_q.
   - sb_valid_q <= !dmem_ready && (sb_valid_q || st). Reset 0. The D input
     is constant 0 when ready=1, so the flop and every mux below vanish.
   - The payload regs capture {alu_result, wdata_rep, byte_mask} every
     cycle while !sb_valid_q, and hold while valid.
   - A store in MEM with !sb_valid_q always completes. If dmem_ready, it
     writes the bus directly as today. Otherwise it is posted: it retires
     normally through MEM/WB and the buffer writes it on a later cycle.
   - Drain has bus priority. While sb_valid_q, the dmem outputs present
     the buffered write (dmem_addr/wdata/wen from sb_*, dmem_ren = 0). The
     write is accepted on the first dmem_ready cycle, and the MEM-stage op
     waits that cycle unless it is a load that hits the cache. Program
     order to memory is preserved (1 entry, FIFO), so UART bytes and the
     0x10000100/104 markers keep their order; a marker is at most a few
     cycles late.
   - dmem_* outputs must stay pure functions of registers (sb_*, EX/MEM),
     never of io_dmemReady. The cosim and cocotb harnesses sample
     WEn/Addr before setting ready.

2. Stall-only load replay cache, 256 entries, direct-mapped, word
   granular: dc_valid[256] (reset), dc_tag[256] = addr[31:10],
   dc_data[256] (resetless). Index = addr[9:2]. Use localparams, not the
   prototype's `ifdef DC_IDX_W`.
   - Fill: on ld_fill, entry[idx(MEM addr)] <= {tag, dmem_rdata}, valid.
   - Store update when st_done (at post time, not drain time, so the cache
     always holds the architectural value). If cand_hit_q or the store is
     a full word, write {tag, merged} and set valid, where
     merged = (cand_data_q & ~lanes(byte_mask)) | (wdata_rep & lanes(byte_mask)).
     Otherwise clear dc_valid[idx] (a defensive invalidate for a partial
     store that misses).
   - Registered lookahead, the same idea as the I-side cand_* registers.
     The table is never read combinationally on a same-cycle ready path.
     On every edge where EX/MEM captures a new entry (ex_adv =
     !stall_ex_mem), cand_hit_q/cand_data_q are loaded for the EX-stage
     address ex_addr (the EX ALU result, exported from ex_stage):
       if (st_done && same_word)      hit <= cand_hit_q || full-word store; data <= merged
       else if (ld_fill && same_word) hit <= 1;                             data <= dmem_rdata
       else                           hit <= dc_valid[x] && dc_tag[x]==ex_addr[31:10]; data <= dc_data[x]
     where same_word = (MEM addr[31:2] == ex_addr[31:2]). While EX/MEM
     holds, cand keeps its value. This is safe because only the MEM-stage
     store can change a word's value, and none completes while MEM holds.
     A same-edge write of the same index for a DIFFERENT word is benign:
     cand is a snapshot of EX's word, and that word is unchanged.
   - Load result: shifted/load_data and MEM/WB.mem_rdata use ld_word
     instead of dmem_rdata. The RVFI mem_rdata is therefore the cached
     architectural word on a hit.
Misaligned (trapping) accesses keep today's behavior: they wait for
bus_free, never fill, never post.

Expected: CoreMark cycles 3,699,911 -> ~3,514,311 (-5.0%) with Fmax
unchanged (all new logic constant-folds), so fitness is ~+5..6%.

lesson: - 2026-09-26 hyp-20260926-002-r4s1 (regression, -1.07%): A stall-only D-side pair (1-entry posted store buffer plus a 256-entry direct-mapped word load cache, updated by every store at post time with a registered EX-address lookahead) delivered its predicted -5.0% CoreMark cycles (3.70M->3.514M, cosim/RVFI-clean) and folded completely out of the io_dmemReady=1 bench netlist (identical cells and FFs before ABC9), yet it scored a regression because ABC9/nextpnr re-rolled the untouched ID/EX->EX adder->EX/MEM path from 162.2 to 152.4 MHz (seeds 145/161/152, while the prototype got 163.9); even a netlist-neutral RTL edit therefore carries about ±6% Fmax noise, more than a 5% cycle win, so re-apply this real, orthogonal gain stacked on the predictor core rather than dropping it, and don't trust a single-netlist Fmax check to confirm it.

title: Fetch predecode + 64-entry bimodal BHT stacked on the I-fetch replay-store core
motivation:
The replay store (hyp-20260926-002-r3s1) removed almost all of the
random-imem-stall cost: 4.49M -> 3,699,911 bracketed cycles, close to the
3.675M dstall-only floor. The biggest remaining overhead is control flow.
The core has no prediction: next PC is always pc+4, and every taken
BRANCH/JAL/JALR redirects from EX with a 1-cycle bubble. That is about
357k bubbles on CoreMark (294k taken branches, 49k JAL, 14k JALR), or
about 9.7% of the current 3.70M cycles.

LESSONS.md says, twice, to put the bimodal predictor on this base
(r1s2 and r3s2). Both times the predictor did what its trace model said
(-6.45% cycles). It was logged as a regression only because it lost to a
sibling in the same round. r3s2 said to predecode instr_word (live or
replayed), steer pc_d so the replay lookahead follows the predicted PC,
and keep kill = flush||redirect on the IF NOP/valid mux. I built that
exact design on a scratch copy of the current cores/bench/rtl (the repo
was not modified) and measured it with the real flow.

  current core (reproduced exactly):  3,699,911 cycles
  + predictor, 64-entry BHT:          3,406,859 cycles (-7.92%)
  BHT size sweep:
    16 entries:   3,425,936
    32 entries:   3,410,548
    64 entries:   3,406,859
    128 entries:  3,410,095 (aliasing)
  64 entries is the knee.
  CRCs match, and "Correct operation validated" is printed.
Correctness:
  - Full RVFI stream under --istall --dstall, cycle field removed: all
    2,937,037 CoreMark retirements are byte-identical to the current
    core's stream.
  - selftest.elf is identical under stalls and passes run_cosim.py.
  - All 20 existing test_pipeline.py cocotb tests pass unchanged,
    including the three replay-store tests.
  - Formal ties imemReady=1, so it sees the same predictor logic that r3s2
    already passed formal with.
FPGA flow: synth.tcl + core_bench_si.sv, then nextpnr_run.sh on seeds
1/2/3.
  - current core:  162.23 / 172.03 / 160.80 MHz (median 162.23)
  - predictor:     166.42 / 160.18 / 155.67 MHz (median 160.18)
  - LUT4 5131 -> 5659, DFF 2098 -> 2253
  - Seeds 1 and 2 are limited by the pre-existing ID/EX -> ALU -> EX/MEM
    path. Seed 3 is limited by the pre-existing, routing-dominated
    ID/EX.rd -> load-use -> ID/EX CE path. No predictor net is on the

(+7.2%).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Predict BRANCH/JAL at fetch from instr_word, the word IF already has this
cycle (live imem_data, or the replayed word on an imem stall). Verify in
EX. Keep today's 1-cycle penalty for mispredicts. JALR stays unpredicted:
a return stack would save only about 14k cycles and would put a 32-bit
compare on the forwarded JALR path.

IF (if_stage.sv): add the predictor next to the existing replay store,
which stays unchanged.
  pd_br  = instr_word[6:0]==7'b1100011 && instr_word[14:13]!=2'b01;  // valid funct3 only
  pd_jal = instr_word[6:0]==7'b1101111;
  pimm   = instr_word[3] ? J-imm(instr_word) : B-imm(instr_word);
  pred_target = pc + pimm;   pc_plus4 = pc + 4;
  ctr    = bht[pc[BHT_IDX_W+1:2]];   // 64 x 2b flop array, sync reset 2'b01
  pred_raw = (pd_jal || (pd_br && ctr[1])) && !pimm[1];  // never predict a misaligned target
  pc_d   = redirect ? redirect_target
         : (!stall ? (pred_raw ? pred_target : pc_plus4) : pc);
The PC flop takes pc_d, and pc_d is also the replay lookahead address. The
replay candidate therefore follows the predicted PC automatically, and
look_keep (pc_d == pc) still covers a predicted self-loop. On a stall the
prediction is dropped, and the same PC is predicted again from the word
fetched next cycle.
Bundle outputs:
  - out.instr and out.valid keep kill = flush || redirect. Do NOT change
    this: r3s2 showed that dropping redirect here makes the
    imem_data -> load-use -> ID/EX CE path critical.
  - out.pred_taken = pred_raw && !(flush || redirect). It must be gated,
    so that bubbles carry pred_taken = 0; otherwise EX fires a false
    redirect.
  - out.bht_ctr = ctr.
  - out.alt_target = pred_raw ? pc_plus4 : pred_target.
BHT write port: inputs bht_we, bht_widx[BHT_IDX_W-1:0], bht_wdata[1:0],
written on the clock edge.

ID (id_stage.sv): latch pred_taken, bht_ctr and alt_target into ID/EX.
The existing reset/flush-to-'0 clears them on bubbles.

EX (ex_stage.sv):
  actual_taken    = (branch_taken || in.ctrl.is_jump) && !misalign_fault;  // today's redirect
  redirect        = actual_taken ^ in.pred_taken;                          // = mispredict
  redirect_target = in.ctrl.is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],1'b0} : in.alt_target;
The last line takes the EX pc+imm adder off the redirect path.
BHT update, registered one cycle after EX so that the forwarded
branch_cond never reaches the BHT write enables:
  bht_we_q    <= in.valid && in.ctrl.is_branch;
  bht_widx_q  <= in.pc[BHT_IDX_W+1:2];
  bht_wdata_q <= branch_cond ? sat_inc(in.bht_ctr) : sat_dec(in.bht_ctr);
Repeated writes while EX is held by a dmem stall or a divide are
idempotent. pc_next, the RVFI fields, the misalign trap and the div_unit
interlock are all unchanged. A divide is never predicted, so redirect
stays 0 while ex_div_busy is high.

core.sv: wire bht_we/bht_widx/bht_wdata from u_ex to u_if.

motivation:

implementation_notes:
# Implementation notes: pre-decoded one-hot ALU controls in ID/EX (predictor core)

## What changed

This is the r3s0 design re-applied to the current replay-store + BHT core. I
made no other edits: IF, the predictor, div_unit, hazard, forwarding, the
regfile and the decoder are untouched.

- `rtl/core_pkg.sv`: new packed `alu_ctl_t` declared before `if_id_t`/`id_ex_t`.
  Fields: sub, sra, mul_a_sgn, mul_b_sgn, sel_sum, sel_and, sel_or, sel_xor,
  sel_slt, sel_sltu, sel_sll, sel_sr, sel_b, sel_mul_lo, sel_mul_hi.
  `id_ex_t` gets `alu_ctl_t alu_ctl` right after `ctrl`. The ALU_* constants
  and `ctrl_t.alu_op` are unchanged, so the decoder and test_decoder are too.
- `rtl/alu.sv` now holds three modules:
  - `alu_predecode(op -> ctl)`: sets `ctl = '0`, then a case on ALU_*.
    DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU and the default leave every bit 0, so the ALU output is 0.
  - `alu_core(ctl, a, b -> out)`:
    - one 33-bit add/sub, `{0,a} + {0, b^{32{sub}}} + sub`
    - `lt_s = (a[31]^b[31]) ? a[31] : sum[31]` and `lt_u = !sum[32]`
    - `a << b[4:0]`
    - one 33-bit `>>>` whose fill bit is `sra & a[31]`
    - one signed product of the sign- or zero-extended operands
    - a one-hot AND-OR result merge
  - `alu(op, a, b -> out)`: the old port list, chaining predecode into core.
    Only `test_alu.py` uses it; the core instantiates the two halves separately.
- ALTOPS: the formulas for MUL, MULH, MULHU and MULHSU are bit-identical to
  before. The ctl sign bits pick the variant: MULH is `mul_b_sgn`, MULHSU is
  `mul_a_sgn` with (a-b), and MULHU is neither.
- `rtl/id_stage.sv`: `alu_predecode u_alu_pd(.op(dec_alu_op))`, registered
  as `reg_q.alu_ctl` inside the existing ID/EX capture. Reset, flush and stall
  work the same as for every other ID/EX field; a bubble has all selects at 0.
- `rtl/ex_stage.sv`: `alu u_alu(.op(in.ctrl.alu_op))` is now
  `alu_core u_alu(.ctl(in.alu_ctl))`. Forwarding, operand muxes, use_alt/alt_val,
  branch/jump resolve, misalign trap, div_unit and the BHT update are unchanged.
- `test/test_alu.py`: five new tests.
  - `slt_sltu_corners`: 0x80000000 vs 0x7fffffff both ways, equal operands,
    0xffffffff vs 0, and similar edge pairs.
  - `add_sub_corners`: wraparound cases for ADD and SUB.
  - `mul_high_corners`: all four MUL variants on INT_MIN*INT_MIN,
    0xffffffff^2, INT_MIN*0xffffffff both ways, 0x7fffffff*INT_MIN both ways,
    and similar.
  - `rv32i_vectors`: every RV32I ALU op against a Python reference, on corner
    and random pairs. This catches a wrong or overlapping one-hot select.
  - `div_ops_output_zero`: the ALU returns 0 for DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU.

## Deviations

- The product operands are written as explicit 66-bit sign extensions,
  `{{34{mul_a_sgn & a[31]}}, a}`. That keeps `verilator -Wall` free of WIDTH
  warnings, and Yosys still maps it to a single MULT36X36.
- `alu.sv` now holds more than one module, so `verilator lint_off DECLFILENAME`
  wraps `alu_predecode`/`alu_core`.

## Concerns

- If you run the literal `verilator ... cores/bench/rtl/*.sv` glob, it
  depends on file order:
  - Under zsh the glob sorts `alu.sv` before `core_pkg.sv`, so the new
    `alu_ctl_t` port type is used before it is declared.
  - Under the C locale, the unmodified parent core already fails the same
    way because `core.sv` sorts before `core_pkg.sv`.

  The orchestrator lint, synth.tcl, cosim build.sh and formal/run_all.sh all
  put `core_pkg.sv` first. In that order lint is clean, with and without
  `-DRISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS`.
- Fmax is sensitive to P&R noise, per LESSONS.md. On the local seeds the ALU
  path is no longer critical. The limiters are now:
  - seed 1: load-use hazard -> ID/EX enable
  - seed 2: div_unit b_q -> neg_q
  - seed 3: regfile -> ID/EX rs data

  All of these are paths that existed before this change.

## Local verification

- Lint (core_pkg.sv first, `-Wall -Wno-MULTITOP`): clean, with and without
  ALTOPS.
- cocotb: all pass.
  - test_alu: 19 ALU tests (5 new) and 15 div_unit tests
  - test_pipeline: 28
  - test_decoder: 31
  - test_imm_gen: 8
  - test_reg_file: 5
- **Formal (`formal/run_all.sh`, nret=1, wrapper_si + checks_si): 53 passed,
  0 failed.**
  - The first run reported `0 passed, 1 failed / no_checks_generated`, even
    though each check that finished logged `DONE (PASS)`. The sibling slot
    (hyp-003-r5s2, CORE_NAME=bench) ran run_all.sh at the same time. Its
    stale-dir cleanup tests each owner PID with `kill -0`, which fails with
    EPERM across sandboxes, so it deleted my live `bench-<pid>` staging dir
    mid-run.
  - I re-ran with `CORE_NAME=r5s0bench` and explicit
    `WRAPPER=formal/wrapper_si.sv CHECKS_CFG=formal/checks_si.cfg`, and got
    53/0. No RTL changed between the two runs.
  - This is a harness race, not an RTL issue. It could hit concurrent
    agent self-checks again.
- CoreMark on Verilator (`--bench --istall --dstall`, 2K, -O3, ITERATIONS=10):
  - bracketed cycles are 3,406,859, identical to the parent core
  - seedcrc 0xe9f5, crclist 0xe714, crcmatrix 0x1fd7, crcstate 0x8e3a,
    crcfinal 0xfcaf
  - "Correct operation validated.", oob=false
- RVFI cosim vs the Python ISS: selftest passed (115 retired); CoreMark passed
  (2,937,037 retired).
- Yosys `synth_gowin` (core_bench_si.sv): 2458 LUT4, 433 MUX2_LUT5, 386 ALU,
  1 MULT36X36.
- nextpnr-himbaechel, eval seeds 1/2/3: **171.20 / 174.46 / 174.76 MHz**,
  median 174.46. The parent's logged median is 156.35 MHz, so this is about
  +11.6% at the same cycle count. Per the lessons, expect the orchestrator's
  netlist to land a few percent below this.
lesson: - 2026-09-26 hyp-20260926-001-r5s0 (improvement, +11.58%): Re-applying r3s0's registered one-hot alu_ctl_t (decode alu_op in ID, AND-OR merge, shared 33-bit add/sub for SLT/SLTU, one 33x33 product) on the predictor core was cycle-identical (3,406,859) and paid off more than twice as much as on the r3 base, because here the ID/EX alu_op -> 4 LUT4 + 3 MUX2_LUT5 decode -> result mux -> EX/MEM path was the same critical path on every seed (seeds reproduced the logged 156.35/146.13 MHz exactly), so removing its logic levels landed in full: the scored fitness matched the local 3-seed median of 174.46 MHz with none of the worst-seed haircut r4s2 saw; so an Fmax change that deletes levels from a seed-stable critical path can be projected from the median, while cycle-only changes on routing-noise-limited paths should still be projected from the worst seed, and the next Fmax targets are the pre-existing load-use hazard -> ID/EX enable, regfile -> ID/EX rs data, and div_unit b_q -> neg_q paths.

title: Speculate load-dependent branches on the BHT prediction and verify them in MEM (no load-use stall)
motivation:
Trace analysis of the current core (CoreMark, --istall --dstall, bracketed
3,406,859 cycles for 2,922,017 retirements, i.e. 484,842 excess cycles) splits the
excess by cause as follows:
  - load-use stalls:         203,959 cycles (6.0% of all cycles)
      load -> BRANCH         135,320  <- this proposal
      load -> load            59,270  (pointer chasing, not predictable)
      load -> ALU/other        9,369
  - dmem random stalls:     ~190k    (memory category, see r4s1)
  - BRANCH mispredicts:       51,846  (1-cycle bubble each: IF feeds ID/EX combinationally)
  - JALR (all are `ret`):     13,735
The obvious predictor upgrades have a low ceiling. On the same trace, a
128..1024-entry bimodal or gshare/gselect (with fetch-visible update lag
modeled) only gets mispredicts down to about 39-42k, a gain of ~10-12k cycles
(0.35%). A return-address stack gains at most 13.7k cycles (0.4%) and would put
a new source on the pc_d mux. The BHT already predicts every BRANCH at fetch,
though, and the branch only needs its operands to *verify* that prediction. Today
a BRANCH that reads the rd of the load right ahead of it takes a full load-use
stall even when the prediction is right. That is 135,320 stalls across 17 static
sites, dominated by 0x484/0x490/0x548/0x550 (~28k each). The 64-entry BHT
predicts 94.7% of these load-dependent branches correctly (128,122 of 135,320).
The operand is almost always rs1: 135,030 rs1-only and 290 rs2.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Let a predicted BRANCH enter EX in the load's shadow without stalling, and check
it one stage later, in MEM, against the load value that is by then registered
in MEM/WB.read_data. A correctly predicted load-dependent branch then costs 0
cycles instead of 1. A mispredicted one costs 2 bubbles (IF + EX killed), which
equals today's 1 stall + 1 redirect bubble, so no case gets slower.

Mechanism (prototyped end to end, see numbers below):
1. hazard_unit: split the load-use compare into ld_rs1 / ld_rs2
   (id_ex.mem_read && id_ex.rd != 0 && id_ex.rd == if_rs1/if_rs2).
   load_use_hazard = (ld_rs1 || ld_rs2) && !if_id_is_branch. New outputs
   late_rs1 = ld_rs1 && if_id_is_branch and late_rs2 = ld_rs2 && if_id_is_branch.
   if_id_is_branch is IF's existing predecode pd_br (BRANCH opcode, funct3 not
   2/3), exported from if_stage as a port; no new decode. Keep the new term shallow:
   it sits in parallel with the 5-bit rd compares on the load-use -> ID/EX CE path.
2. id_stage: ID/EX latches late_rs1 / late_rs2 (reset/flush clear them).
3. ex_stage: late = late_rs1 || late_rs2. For a late branch the EX compare used
   a stale operand (the load's address, forwarded from EX/MEM), so:
   redirect = !late && (actual_taken ^ pred_taken), and misalign_branch also
   requires !late. New input `kill` (= the MEM late redirect) makes EX a wrong-path
   slot: EX/MEM captures valid=0, ctrl='0 (a wrong-path STORE must never reach
   MEM, since dmem_wen is combinational from EX/MEM) and late flags 0, and the
   div_unit start is gated with !kill. EX/MEM additionally carries branch_cond,
   tgt_misalign (branch_target[1:0]!=0), pred_taken, bht_ctr, alt_target, and
   late_rs1/late_rs2.
4. mem_stage (the verify step): late = in.valid && (late_rs1 || late_rs2).
   op1 = late_rs1 ? reg_q.read_data : in.rs1_val, and likewise op2. The load
   and the branch always advance in lockstep (EX/MEM only holds for a memory op,
   and a branch has none), so MEM/WB is exactly the load. Six-way compare on
   op1/op2 gives cond_late. taken_late = cond_late && !tgt_misalign.
   replay = !reg_q.ctrl.reg_write (the load did not write, i.e. a misaligned-load
   trap). redirect = late && (replay || (taken_late ^ pred_taken)), with
   target = replay ? in.pc : in.alt_target. On replay the branch captures
   valid=0 into MEM/WB and is refetched with no hazard, so liveness holds.
   MEM/WB gets the corrected rs1_val/rs2_val (op1/op2) for RVFI, the corrected
   pc_next (taken_late ? branch_target : pc+4), and is_illegal |= cond_late &&
   tgt_misalign. Every source here is a register (MEM/WB.read_data, EX/MEM),
   so the new compare -> redirect path is shorter than EX's forward-mux ->
   compare path.
5. BHT write port moves from EX to MEM (one port, registered, written the next
   cycle) for *all* branches: cond = late ? cond_late : in.branch_cond, and
   we = valid && is_branch && !(late && replay). A branch is in EX/MEM for exactly
   one cycle and only correct-path instructions reach it, so the "idempotent
   repeated write while EX is held" caveat and wrong-path BHT pollution both go
   away. A trace replay with update lag 3/4/5 cycles gives the identical 51,846
   mispredicts.
6. core.sv: redirect = mem_redirect || ex_redirect, and
   redirect_target = mem_redirect ? mem_target : ex_target (MEM is older, so it
   wins). Feed this into IF and hazard_unit as today, and kill = mem_redirect
   into ex_stage.

Prototype results (scratch copy of rtl/: 7 files, +147/-52 lines):
  - CoreMark bracketed cycles 3,406,859 -> 3,278,562 (-3.77%). The trace model
    predicted -128,122; the prototype measured -128,297. CRCs and "Correct
    operation validated" are OK.
  - RVFI streams are byte-identical to the current core's (CoreMark with and
    without istall/dstall; selftest under all 4 stall modes), except mem_rdata
    on non-memory retirements (rmask=0): it is the raw bus word sampled at an
    address formed from the late branch's stale EX operand. It is a don't-care

title: LUT-RAM register file + ID/EX control/data split + registered div b!=0 (Fmax 174 -> ~223 MHz, cycle-identical)
motivation:
I re-ran yosys + 3-seed nextpnr on the current best RTL (r5s0, 512.08 =
10 / 3,406,859 cycles x 174.46 MHz). It reproduces the logged
171.20 / 174.46 / 174.76 MHz exactly. The three seeds end on three different
pre-existing paths, and each has 55-60% routing delay:
  seed 1 (5.84 ns): ID/EX.rd -> load-use compare (5 LUT levels) -> stall/flush
          -> CE of the ~240-flop ID/EX register. The last two hops are 2.35 ns of
          routing (fanout).
  seed 2 (5.73 ns): div_unit b_q -> 32-bit (b_q != 0) OR tree -> res_neg -> neg_q.
  seed 3 (5.72 ns): regfile flop regs[4] -> 6 LUT/MUX levels of 32:1 read mux ->
          write-first bypass -> ID/EX rs_val.
The register file is the dominant hidden cost. reg_file.sv resets all 32 regs
in a for-loop, so yosys cannot infer memory. It builds 992 DFFE flops plus two
32:1 LUT-mux read trees, which is about 60% of all LUTs in the design. That
inflates the placement and the routing distance on every other path too.

Prototype (scratch copy of rtl/, all numbers measured with the eval's own
synth.tcl + nextpnr_run.sh, core_bench_si.sv, seeds 1/2/3):
  base (r5s0):              171.20 / 174.46 / 174.76 MHz
  + resetless regfile:      183.39 / 162.31 / 202.96 MHz. Yosys now maps it to
                            32 RAM16SDP4 (LUT RAM). LUT1-4 go 5152 -> 2419 and
                            DFFE 1121 -> 128. Now EVERY seed ends on the
                            load-use -> ID/EX CE path.
  + ID/EX control/data split
  + registered div b != 0:  227.48 / 222.32 / 223.51 MHz (median 223.51, +28.1%)
With all three changes, the limiters are about 4.4-4.5 ns paths that no longer
share a common structure: the div ITER 33-bit restoring subtract (seed 1) and
EX/MEM.rd -> forward select -> fwd mux -> div_unit start neg_q (seeds 2 and 3).
Cycle count is unchanged and RVFI is clean. On the Verilator cosim build
(--bench --istall --dstall) the bracketed cycles are 3,406,859, byte-identical
to r5s0. The CoreMark CRCs are all correct, "Correct operation validated", and
oob=false. run_cosim.py vs the Python ISS passes on selftest (115 retired) and
on CoreMark (2,937,037 retired).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three micro-optimizations. None of them changes the cycle count.

1. LUT-RAM register file (rtl/reg_file.sv). Delete the reset for-loop so the
   write is a plain `if (w_en && w_addr != 0) regs[w_addr] <= w_data;`. Yosys
   synth_gowin then infers 32 x RAM16SDP4 (two read ports = replicated
   banks). Keep the combinational read, the x0 -> 0 read override, and the
   write-first bypass exactly as they are. The `reset` port can stay (tie it to
   an unused-signal sink for lint) or be removed from the module and from
   core.sv. RISC-V does not require GPRs to reset. Verilator zero-initializes
   them, which is what cosim, CoreMark and run_cosim.py already rely on (the
   prototype passed all three). riscv-formal's reg check tracks
   written-before-read and does not assume reset values. The BHT/replay
   tag/data arrays are already resetless memories and pass formal.

2. ID/EX control/data split (rtl/id_stage.sv, rtl/hazard_unit.sv,
   rtl/core.sv). Today all ~240 ID/EX bits share sync-reset (reset || flush)
   and enable (!stall_id). stall_id and flush_id both come from
   load_use_hazard and redirect, so that late net fans out to every bit. Only
   the bits with side effects need to be cleared to make a bubble.
   - Control half: 8 flops. valid, pred_taken, ctrl.reg_write, ctrl.mem_read,
     ctrl.mem_write, ctrl.is_branch, ctrl.is_jump, ctrl.is_div.
     They are cleared on reset || flush_id; otherwise they capture when
     !hold_id.
   - Data half: every other field (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs1/rs2
     addr, the rest of ctrl, alu_ctl, instr, bht_ctr, alt_target). It has no
     reset and captures when !hold_id.
   - hazard_unit replaces the stall_id output with hold_id = dmem_stall ||
     ex_div_busy. It drops load_use from the enable. This is equivalent
     because load_use without dmem_stall already forces flush_id, and
     load_use with dmem_stall is inside hold_id. flush_id is unchanged.
   - Compose `out` combinationally: out = data_q with those 8 fields overridden
     by the control flops. Use separate registers, not two always_ff blocks
     writing one packed struct (multi-driver).
   - Why a bubble with a stale payload is safe:
     - EX's side effects all key off the 8 cleared bits: redirect needs
       is_branch/is_jump/pred_taken; the misalign trap needs
       is_branch/is_jump; the BHT write needs valid && is_branch; the divide
       start needs valid && is_div.
     - Forwarding, load-use and dmem enables all key off
       reg_write/mem_read/mem_write.
     - RVFI keys off valid.
     - A bubble's alu_result may be arbitrary, but dmem_ren/wen are 0 and
       reg_write is 0.
   - Net effect: load_use and redirect now drive the sync-clear of 8 flops,
     plus the PC hold, instead of the CE/SR pins of ~240 flops.

3. div_unit b == 0 off the neg_q path (rtl/div_unit.sv). In PREP, register
   b_nz_q <= (b_q != 0) and set neg_q <= is_rem_q ? a_neg : (a_neg ^ b_neg).
   In ITER, fold neg_q <= neg_q && (is_rem_q || b_nz_q). This is idempotent
   across all 32 ITER cycles, and neg_q is not read again until FIXUP. The
   32-bit zero detect becomes its own FF->FF path. Real-arithmetic results
   are unchanged, and the ALTOPS path (PREP -> DONE) never reads neg_q. The
   header comment already describes a registered b_zero; make the code match.

Expected: cycles 3,406,859 (unchanged). The 3-seed median is about 220 MHz
(prototype 222.3-227.5), so fitness is about 10 / 3.407M x 220e6 = ~646
(+26%). This change deletes levels and fanout from seed-stable paths (the
r5s0 pattern) and does not rely on routing luck. Projecting from the prototype's
worst seed (222.3 MHz) still gives +27%.

title: Stall-only D-side: 1-entry posted store buffer + 256-entry load replay cache on the one-hot-ALU core
motivation:
The fitness run counts cycles in cosim with ~22% random refusals on BOTH
buses, but measures Fmax on core_bench_si.sv, which ties io_imemReady and
io_dmemReady to 1. The I side is already solved: the r3s1 replay store
(+22.1%) folds out of the bench netlist. The D side is not. Any
io_dmemReady=0 cycle with a LOAD/STORE in EX/MEM still freezes the whole
pipeline.

I measured this on the current cores/bench RTL (test/cosim/build.sh,
NRET=1, coremark.elf --bench, bracketed cycles):
  --istall --dstall : 3,406,859   (= logged current best, 512.08)
  --istall only     : 3,216,666
  --dstall only     : 3,382,321
  no stalls         : 3,191,647
So dstall costs 190,193 cycles, 5.58% of the scored run. That is now the
largest single overhead: load->branch stalls are ~135k (predictor slot,
r5s2), and mispredicts ~52k.

r4s1 already built and fully validated exactly this D-side pair on the
replay-store core:
- Cycles dropped 3,699,911 -> 3,514,311 (-5.0%), within 6k of the
  istall-only floor.
- RVFI diff passed on all 2.94M CoreMark retirements under several seeds.
- Every new cell folded out of the dmemReady=1 bench netlist (sb_valid_q
  aliased to GND, no dc_/cand_/sb_ cells).
It scored "regression" only because ABC9/nextpnr re-rolled an untouched
path (162 -> 152 MHz) on that older, noisier core, and because the
predictor and one-hot-ALU siblings won those rounds. LESSONS.md
(r4s1, r4s2) names it the next orthogonal cycle win to stack.

The program and data trace are unchanged: 611 unique data words, 80% of
dmem accesses are loads, and a 256-entry direct-mapped word cache hits
97.2%. So the same ~184k saving should land on today's 3.41M base.
Today's base is also a better place for it. Its three seeds are tight
(171.2 / 174.5 / 174.8 MHz) because the critical path was removed at the
logic level, not by routing luck.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Re-apply hyp-20260926-002-r4s1 on the current core. It adds two stall-only
structures in MEM. They are used ONLY on cycles when the external bus
cannot serve the MEM-stage access. With io_dmemReady tied to 1 (FPGA
bench, formal wrapper), every new state bit either has a constant D input
or feeds only dead logic, so the synthesized netlist folds back to
today's.

Definitions (mem_stage, combinational):
  ld        = ctrl.mem_read  && !mem_misalign      (= today's dmem_ren)
  st        = ctrl.mem_write && !mem_misalign
  bus_free  = dmem_ready && !sb_valid_q    (bus serves the MEM op now)
  st_done   = st && !sb_valid_q    (store written directly, or posted)
  ld_fill   = ld && bus_free && cacheable
  ld_word   = bus_free ? dmem_rdata : cand_data_q
  mem_ready = bus_free || (ld && cand_hit_q) || st_done
  cacheable = !alu_result[28]   (never cache the MMIO/UART/marker window)
In hazard_unit, dmem_stall becomes !mem_ready && ex_mem_mem_op, replacing
!dmem_ready. Every other stall/flush/hold equation and priority stays as
it is, including hold_mem_wb and redirect-over-stall in IF.

1. Posted store buffer (1 entry): sb_valid_q, sb_addr_q, sb_wdata_q
   (replicated lanes), sb_wmask_q.
   - sb_valid_q <= !dmem_ready && (sb_valid_q || st). It resets to 0.
     With ready=1 its D input is constant 0, so the flop and every mux
     behind it vanish.
   - The payload regs capture {alu_result, wdata_rep, byte_mask} every
     cycle while !sb_valid_q, and hold while it is valid.
   - A store in MEM always completes when !sb_valid_q. If dmem_ready, it
     writes the bus directly, as today. Otherwise it is posted: it
     retires normally through MEM/WB and the buffer writes it later.
   - The drain has bus priority. While sb_valid_q, the dmem outputs
     present the buffered write (addr/wdata/wen from sb_*, ren = 0). The
     write is accepted on the first dmem_ready cycle. The MEM-stage op
     waits that cycle unless it is a load that hits the cache.
   - With one entry the buffer is FIFO, so memory sees stores in program
     order. UART bytes and the 0x10000100/104 markers keep their order;
     a marker lands at most a few cycles late.
   - dmem_addr/wdata/wen/ren must be pure functions of registers (sb_*,
     EX/MEM), never of io_dmemReady. The harnesses sample them before
     they drive ready.

2. Stall-only load replay cache: 256 entries, direct-mapped, one word
   per entry. dc_valid[256] is reset; dc_tag[256] = addr[31:10] and
   dc_data[256] are resetless. Index = addr[9:2]. Use localparams.
   - Fill: on ld_fill, entry[idx] <= {tag, dmem_rdata} and set valid.
   - Store update: on st_done, at post time (not drain time), so the
     cache always holds the architectural value.
     - If the store is cacheable and (cand_hit_q or a full word): write
       {tag, merged} and set valid, where
       merged = (cand_data_q & ~lanes(mask)) | (wdata_rep & lanes(mask)).
     - Otherwise clear dc_valid[idx] (defensive invalidate for a
       partial-store miss).
   - Registered lookahead, the same pattern as the I-side cand_*
     registers. The table is never read combinationally on a
     ready-path.
     - On every edge where EX/MEM captures a new entry
       (ex_adv = !stall_ex_mem), load cand_hit_q/cand_data_q for
       ex_addr, the EX ALU result exported from ex_stage:
         if (st_done && same_word) hit <= cacheable && (cand_hit_q || full word); data <= merged
         else if (ld_fill && same_word) hit <= 1; data <= dmem_rdata
         else hit <= dc_valid[x] && dc_tag[x] == ex_addr[31:10] && !ex_addr[28]; data <= dc_data[x]
       where same_word = (MEM addr[31:2] == ex_addr[31:2]).
     - While EX/MEM holds, cand keeps its value. This is safe because
       only the MEM-stage store can change a word, and none completes
       while MEM holds. A same-edge write to the same index for a
       different word is benign.
   - Load result: the load extraction and MEM/WB.mem_rdata use ld_word
     instead of dmem_rdata. On a hit, RVFI mem_rdata is the cached
     architectural word.
   - Coherence: dmem has exactly one master (this core), imem is a
     separate port, and every store updates the cache, so the cache is
     coherent by construction. The core never consumes io_dmemRData on
     a refused cycle, and MMIO words are never cached.

Misaligned (trapping) accesses keep today's behavior: they wait for
bus_free, never fill, and never post.

Expected result:
- CoreMark cycles 3,406,859 -> ~3,222,000 (-5.4%), within ~6k of the
  3,216,666 istall-only floor, as r4s1 was.
- Every new cell constant-folds in the bench netlist (LUT4/FF counts
  ~unchanged), so Fmax is today's 171-175 MHz modulo P&R noise.
- Fitness ~ 10 / 3.222M x 174.5 MHz = ~541 (+5.7%) at the median seed;
  +3.8% even at 171.2 MHz, the current worst seed.
- The change is orthogonal to the predictor-slot work (IF/EX/load-use)
  and stacks with it later.

The implementer should confirm in the synthesized core_bench_si netlist
that sb_valid_q is constant and no dc_/cand_/sb_ cells survive. They
should run the 3 eval seeds, not a single one.

lesson: - 2026-09-26 hyp-20260926-002-r7s1 (regression, +2.94%): Re-applying r4s1's stall-only D-side pair (1-entry posted store buffer + 256-entry load replay cache, MMIO window bit 28 never cached) on the r5s0 one-hot-ALU core finally scored above its base (527.14 vs 512.08), but only about half the projected +5.7%: if the expected ~3.22M cycles landed, the score implies ~170 MHz, just under that core's worst seed (171.2), which is the ~3% haircut r4s1/r4s2 already saw on cycle-only changes, and it lost the round to r7s0's LUT-RAM register file (+25.65%); a cycle-only win that folds out of the bench netlist keeps losing to same-round Fmax restructures, so stack it once more on the r7s0 core, whose seed-stable limiter is load-use/redirect -> ID/EX CE, but first confirm there that the new dmem_stall = !mem_ready && mem_op still folds to 0 with io_dmemReady=1, because dmem_stall now feeds hold_id, the enable of that ~240-flop register.

title: Speculate load-dependent branches on the BHT and verify in MEM, re-applied on the one-hot-ALU core with the load-use CE and redirect paths kept flat
motivation:
The current best core (r5s0, 512.08) runs CoreMark in 3,406,859 bracketed
cycles for 2,922,017 retirements. Its 3-seed Fmax is 171.2 / 174.46 / 174.76 MHz.
r5s2 did a trace breakdown of the ~485k excess cycles on this exact cycle
count. r5s0 did not change the count, so the breakdown still holds:
  - load-use stalls: 203,959
      load -> BRANCH   135,320  (17 static sites; 0x484/0x490/0x548/0x550 ~28k each)
      load -> load      59,270  (pointer chasing)
      load -> other      9,369
  - dmem random stalls: ~190k (memory category)
  - BRANCH mispredicts: 51,846 (1 bubble each)
  - JALR/ret:           13,735
The other predictor upgrades have low ceilings. On the same trace, gshare or
gselect up to 1024 entries saves only ~10-12k cycles (0.35%). A RAS saves at
most 13.7k cycles (0.4%) and would add a source to the pc_d mux.

The IF-stage BHT already predicts every one of those 135k load-dependent
branches at fetch, and gets 94.7% of them right (128,122). The branch only
needs the loaded value to verify that prediction, not to steer fetch.
r5s2 built this on r4s2. It measured -128,297 cycles (3,406,859 ->
3,278,562, -3.77%) with an RVFI stream byte-identical to the base and no
new logic on any critical path. It scored "regression" only because
its sibling r5s0 won the same round. LESSONS.md says to re-apply it on
the r5s0 core, but first make sure the new !is_branch term does not
lengthen the load-use hazard -> ID/EX enable path. That path was the r5s0
seed-1 limiter. This hypothesis does that re-apply and makes the timing
guard explicit.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Let a BRANCH that reads the rd of the LOAD right ahead of it enter EX
without the load-use stall. Its EX compare runs on a stale operand, so EX
neither redirects nor traps it. One stage later, in MEM, compare against the
registered MEM/WB.read_data. A correctly predicted load-dependent branch then
costs 0 cycles instead of 1. A mispredicted one costs 2 bubbles (IF slot and
EX slot killed), the same as today's 1 stall + 1 redirect bubble. No case
gets slower.

Mechanism (the r5s2 design, validated end to end on r4s2):
1. hazard_unit: split the match into ld_rs1 / ld_rs2. Then
   load_use_hazard = (ld_rs1 || ld_rs2) && !if_id_is_branch,
   late_rs1 = ld_rs1 && if_id_is_branch, and likewise late_rs2.
   if_id_is_branch is IF's existing predecode pd_br (BRANCH opcode, funct3
   not 2/3), exported as a port. It must be qualified by IF's kill, or
   come from out.instr, which is already a NOP when killed.
2. id_stage: ID/EX latches late_rs1 / late_rs2. Reset and flush clear them.
3. ex_stage: late = late_rs1 || late_rs2 suppresses the EX redirect and
   misalign_branch. New input kill (= the MEM redirect) makes the EX slot
   wrong-path: EX/MEM captures valid=0, ctrl='0 (a wrong-path STORE must
   never reach MEM, because dmem_wen is combinational from EX/MEM) and late
   flags 0, and the div_unit start is gated with !kill. EX/MEM also carries
   branch_cond, tgt_misalign (branch_target[1:0] != 0), pred_taken,
   bht_ctr, alt_target, late_rs1 and late_rs2.
4. mem_stage verify: late = in.valid && (late_rs1 || late_rs2).
   op1 = late_rs1 ? MEM/WB.read_data : in.rs1_val, and likewise op2.
   The load and the branch move in lockstep: EX/MEM holds only for a
   memory op, and hold_wb keeps read_data alive. So MEM/WB is exactly the
   load. A six-way compare gives cond_late, and
   taken_late = cond_late && !tgt_misalign.
   replay = !MEM/WB.ctrl.reg_write (misaligned-load trap).
   mem_redirect = late && (replay || (taken_late ^ pred_taken)), with
   target = replay ? pc : alt_target.
   MEM/WB gets the corrected rs1_val/rs2_val (for RVFI) and the corrected
   pc_next. It also gets is_illegal |= cond_late && tgt_misalign, and
   valid=0 on replay.
5. The BHT write port moves from EX to MEM for all branches: registered,
   written the next cycle, cond = late ? cond_late : branch_cond. A branch
   sits in EX/MEM for exactly one cycle and only correct-path
   instructions reach it. That removes the repeated write while EX is held
   and any wrong-path pollution. Trace replay at update lags 3/4/5 gives
   identical mispredict counts.
6. core.sv: MEM is older, so its redirect wins over EX's. kill =
   mem_redirect goes into ex_stage.

New on this core: timing guards for the paths r5s0 is limited by.
(a) Load-use -> ID/EX CE (the r5s0 seed-1 critical path). Register
    ld_nz = ctrl.mem_read && (rd != 0) in the ID/EX register. The stall's
    final gate is then the 4-input function {ld_nz, eq_rs1, eq_rs2, pd_br},
    the same depth as today's {mem_read, eq_rs1, eq_rs2, rd_nz}. pd_br
    (7 opcode bits + funct3[2:1]) is computed in parallel with the 5-bit
    rd compares and is not in series with them. late_rs1/late_rs2 feed only
    ID/EX D inputs, never the CE.
(b) Redirect. Fold mem_redirect into the final redirect gate as one
    expression (ex: actual_taken ^ pred_taken, gated by !late; OR
    mem_redirect) so ABC can merge it into the existing LUT instead of adding
    a level. For the target mux, keep jalr_sum (forward mux -> adder, the
    late arrival) at one mux level. Use
    target = (is_jalr && !mem_redirect) ? jalr_sum : (mem_redirect ? mem_target : alt_target).
    The inner mux and the select come only from registers and the short
    MEM compare.
(c) Every MEM verify source (MEM/WB.read_data, EX/MEM fields) is a
    register, so the MEM compare -> redirect path is shorter than EX's
    forward mux -> compare path.

Expected: cycles 3,406,859 -> ~3,278,600 (-3.77%, model and prototype
agreed within 175 cycles). That is +3.9% fitness at equal Fmax. The
r5s2 prototype's Fmax did not drop on its base (median 156.35 -> 162.58,
i.e. noise). About +300 LUT4 and +50 FF (5,560 -> ~5,860, well under the
10k target). None of this logic reaches the imem/dmem ready paths, so
there is no interaction with the replay store's constant-folding.
One RVFI don't-care: for non-memory retirements (rmask=0), mem_rdata may
differ. Neither run_cosim.py nor riscv-formal checks it.
